_comment: Math response garnishes v1. One-line asides appended to COMPUTE answers ~20% of the time, when the answer matches the trigger pattern. Slot syntax {SLOT:theme} works if needed but most entries are pure plain text.

garnishes.text: (zero — Indian mathematicians worked out the idea of nothing-as-a-number around 600 CE)
(one — the multiplicative identity, multiply anything by it and it stays itself)
(seven — prime and indivisible, lucky in many cultures)
(twelve — a dozen, and divisible by 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 12)
(thirteen — a baker's dozen, and prime)
(forty-two — the answer to life, the universe, and everything, per Douglas Adams)
(sixty — minutes in an hour, seconds in a minute, base-60 inherited from the Sumerians)
(one hundred — a century, and a whole percent)
(144 — a gross, old word for twelve dozen)
(256 — two to the eighth, the number of values one byte can hold)
(512 — two to the ninth, half a kilobyte in the old reckoning)
(1024 — two to the tenth, and that's why a kilobyte used to mean 1024 bytes)
(pi — the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, never ending and never repeating)
(e — the natural growth constant, shows up wherever things grow at a rate proportional to their size)
(phi — the golden ratio, found in spirals from seashells to sunflowers)
(infinity — not a number but a direction, and some infinities are bigger than others)
(handy that 25% is just a quarter — divide by 4)
(50% is half — divide by 2)
(75% is three-quarters — multiply by 3, divide by 4)
(10% is just shift the decimal point left one place — sneaky shortcut)
(square root means 'what number times itself gives this')
(logs ask 'what power of 10 makes this?')
(ln is the natural log — base e, the calculus-friendly one)
(factorial: each step multiplies by one more)
(trig: ratios of sides in a right triangle)
(squaring makes positives bigger and negatives positive)
(cubing keeps the sign — negatives stay negative)
(speed is just distance divided by time)
(primes are the atoms of numbers — every whole number breaks down into them)
(GCD — the biggest number that divides both cleanly)
(LCM — the smallest number both divide into cleanly)
(division is just asking how many times one number fits inside another)
(if you want the work shown, just add 'step by step')
(want me to explain the concept? type 'how does this work?')
(rounded to a couple of decimals — say so if you want more)
(if you need exact, ask for the fraction)
(neat little number, that one)
(one of those satisfying answers)
(answers don't get cleaner than that)
(want a story about a number that does this?)
(a quick estimate is always a good sanity check)
(math, when you squint, is just patterns waiting to be noticed)
(1 ft is about 0.3048 m — a foot is roughly a third of a meter)
(F = C times 9/5 plus 32. 0 C is 32 F, 100 C is 212 F)
(C = (F minus 32) times 5/9 — subtract 32 first, then scale)
(the mile comes from Roman 'mille passus' — a thousand paces)
(the meter was originally defined as one ten-millionth of the distance from the equator to the north pole)
(an inch was historically the width of a thumb)
(a kilogram was once defined by a single metal cylinder in a vault near Paris)
(two — the only even prime, the loneliest of its kind)
(three — the smallest number you can draw a polygon with)
(six — the first perfect number: its divisors 1, 2, and 3 add right back up to it)
(nine — multiply it by anything and the digits of the answer add back to a multiple of nine)
(ten — we count in tens almost certainly because we have ten fingers)
(eleven — the smallest two-digit prime, and a palindrome to boot)
(sixteen — two to the fourth, and the number of digits in hexadecimal)
(twenty-one — a triangular number: stack 1+2+3+4+5+6 and you get it)
(twenty-eight — the second perfect number, equal to the sum of its proper divisors)
(360 — degrees in a circle, a count we inherited from Babylonian base-60 math)
(365 — days in a year, give or take the quarter-day we save up for leap years)
(666 — it's the sum of all the numbers on a roulette wheel, 0 through 36)
(one thousand — 'kilo' comes from the Greek 'khilioi' meaning exactly this)
(the square root of two — proving it can't be a fraction supposedly upset the ancient Greeks)
(the square root of three — it shows up in the height of an equilateral triangle)
(the Euler-Mascheroni constant — and to this day nobody knows if it's even irrational)
(modulo gives the leftover after division — it's how clocks wrap around at 12)
(Fibonacci: each number is the sum of the two before it, and the ratios creep toward the golden ratio)
(the mean adds everything up and shares it out evenly)
(the median is the middle value — outliers can't drag it around like they do the mean)
(combinations count groups where order doesn't matter — picking the same friends in any order is one group)
(permutations care about order — ABC and CBA count as different arrangements)
(rounding: five and up rounds up, four and down rounds down)
(two negatives multiplied make a positive — turning around twice points you forward again)
(a derivative measures how fast something is changing right at one instant)
(an integral adds up infinitely many tiny slices to find a total area)
(zero, infinity, and the rest — every number has a tiny story)
(the answer doesn't change no matter how many times you check it — that's the comfort of math)
(want it in a different unit? just ask)
(I never get tired of a clean calculation)
(pi is irrational, so its digits never repeat and never end — they just keep going 🐒)
(that's the golden ratio — it shows up in sunflower spirals and pinecones)
(6 is a perfect number — its divisors 1, 2, and 3 add right back up to 6)
(28 is the second perfect number: 1+2+4+7+14 = 28)
(360 has 24 divisors, which is why ancient folks loved it for splitting a circle)
(fun fact: the mean can be yanked around by one outlier, but the median shrugs it off)
(in a bell curve, about 68% of the data lands within one standard deviation of the mean)
(the median is just the middle value once you line everything up in order)
(2 is the only even prime — every other even number has 2 as a factor 🐒)
(1 isn't prime — primes need exactly two divisors, and 1 only has itself)
(a triangle's three angles always add up to 180 degrees on a flat surface)
(every circle's circumference divided by its diameter equals pi — every single one)
(bees build hexagons because they tile a wall with the least wax for the most space)
(3-4-5 is the friendliest right triangle: 9 + 16 = 25, exactly)
(a sphere holds the most volume for its surface area — that's why bubbles are round)
(7 is the only number from 1–10 you can't make a regular polygon's angle land on neatly... and people just love it)
(12 is a 'highly composite' number — it has more divisors than any smaller number)
(100 is a perfect square: 10 times 10 🐒)
(in Fibonacci, each number is the sum of the two before it — and their ratios creep toward the golden ratio)
(all the probabilities of every possible outcome always add up to exactly 1)
